en: Angular Dependence of the Wavefunction

p.src: A particle in a central force field has a radial position and two angular coordinates. Classically, $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p$ is conserved as a vector. Its direction fixes the plane of the orbit, although the orbit need not be circular.

p.src: Quantum mechanically the particle is described by $\Psi=\Psi(r,\theta,\phi),$ and angular momentum concerns the dependence of this wavefunction on the angles.

u.src: Quantum mechanically the particle is described by $\Psi=\Psi(r,\theta,\phi),$ and angular momentum concerns the dependence of this wavefunction on the angles.
en: Quantum mechanically the particle is described by $\Psi=\Psi(r,\theta,\phi),$ and angular momentum concerns the dependence of this wavefunction on the angles.

p.src:
In two dimensions there is only one angular-momentum component, the generator of rotations about the axis perpendicular to the plane: $L_z=-i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}.$ An eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\hbar\ell$ obeys $-i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\psi(r,\theta)
=\hbar\ell\,\psi(r,\theta).$ The coordinate $r$ is a spectator in this equation. Its solution has the form $\psi(r,\theta)=\chi(r)e^{i\ell\theta}.$ For an ordinary single-valued orbital wavefunction, returning to the same point after $\theta\to\theta+2\pi$ requires $\ell$ to be an integer. The radial factor $\chi(r)$ may affect the energy, but it does not affect this angular-momentum eigenvalue.

p.src: Finite Angular-Momentum Multiplets

u.src: Finite Angular-Momentum Multiplets
en: Finite Angular-Momentum Multiplets

p.src:
The components of angular momentum satisfy $\begin{aligned}
[L_x,L_y]&=i\hbar L_z,\\
[L_y,L_z]&=i\hbar L_x,\\
[L_z,L_x]&=i\hbar L_y.
\end{aligned}$ Choose eigenstates of $L_z$, $L_z|\ell,m\rangle=\hbar m\,|\ell,m\rangle,$ and define $L_\pm=L_x\pm iL_y.$ The commutators $=\pm\hbar L_\pm$ give $\begin{aligned}
L_z\bigl(L_\pm|\ell,m\rangle\bigr)
&=\bigl(L_\pm L_z+[L_z,L_\pm]\bigr)|\ell,m\rangle \\
&=\hbar(m\pm1)L_\pm|\ell,m\rangle.\end{aligned}$ Thus $L_+$ raises $m$ by one and $L_-$ lowers it by one, unless the resulting vector vanishes.

p.src:
For a finite multiplet there is a highest state and a lowest state: $L_+|\ell,\ell\rangle=0,
\qquad
L_-|\ell,-\ell\rangle=0.$ The $+z$ and $-z$ directions are related by a rotation, so the finite spectrum is symmetric about zero. Its values are therefore $m=-\ell,-\ell+1,\ldots,\ell-1,\ell,$ and the number of states is $2\ell+1.$ Since neighboring values differ by one, the endpoints can be integers or half-integers. Ordinary orbital spherical harmonics realize the integer case; the abstract angular-momentum algebra also permits half-integer multiplets.

p.src: The Common Value of $L^2$

u.src: The Common Value of $L^2$
en: The Common Value of $L^2$

p.src:
The operator measuring the square of the angular-momentum magnitude is $L^2=L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2.$ The ordered product of ladder operators is $\begin{aligned}
L_-L_+
&=(L_x-iL_y)(L_x+iL_y) \\
&=L_x^2+L_y^2+i[L_x,L_y] \\
&=L_x^2+L_y^2-\hbar L_z.\end{aligned}$ Consequently, $L^2=L_z^2+\hbar L_z+L_-L_+.$ Apply this identity to the highest state. Since $L_+|\ell,\ell\rangle=0$, $\begin{aligned}
L^2|\ell,\ell\rangle
&=\left(L_z^2+\hbar L_z+L_-L_+\right)|\ell,\ell\rangle \\
&=\hbar^2\left(\ell^2+\ell\right)|\ell,\ell\rangle,\end{aligned}$ and therefore $L^2|\ell,\ell\rangle
=\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)|\ell,\ell\rangle.$ The squared magnitude is not $\hbar^2\ell^2$. The extra term is a consequence of the noncommutativity of the angular-momentum components.

p.src: Consider $H=\frac{\mathbf p^2}{2m}+V(r),$ where $V$ depends only on the distance from the origin. Rotational symmetry implies conservation of angular momentum. Classically, $\mathbf L$ has fixed magnitude and direction, so the orbit remains in a plane perpendicular to $\mathbf L$. The orbit need not be circular, or even closed.

p.src: Choose coordinates so that this classical orbital plane is the $xy$-plane, and resolve the momentum into radial and tangential components: $\mathbf p^2=p_r^2+p_\theta^2.$ Since the magnitude of the angular momentum is $L=r p_\theta,$ the tangential contribution may be written $p_\theta^2=\frac{L^2}{r^2}.$ The Hamiltonian becomes $H=\frac{p_r^2}{2m}+\frac{L^2}{2mr^2}+V(r).$ For fixed $L$, this is a one-dimensional problem in the radial coordinate, with effective potential $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)=\frac{L^2}{2mr^2}+V(r).$ The radial Hamiltonian is shown on the blackboard below.

p.src: The $1/r^2$ term is the centrifugal barrier. It rises as the particle approaches the origin, so the associated force points outward. For the Coulomb-like attractions under discussion, a trajectory with $L\neq0$ swings around the center instead of reaching it. When $L=0$, the barrier is absent.

p.src: For the attractive Coulomb potential, $V(r)=-\frac{\kappa}{r},$ the centrifugal term dominates at small $r$, while the Coulomb term falls more slowly and dominates at large $r$. For $L\neq0$, their sum has a minimum. Motion at the minimum has constant radius and is therefore circular. Bound motion above the minimum and below the escape threshold oscillates between a smallest and a largest radius; in the Coulomb problem these are the radial oscillations of an elliptical orbit.

p.src: For fixed $\ell$, the reduced radial equation is an ordinary one-dimensional eigenvalue problem. Its bound states are ordered by their number of interior nodes. The lowest radial state has no interior node, the next has one, and the next has two. More nodes mean more rapid variation of the wavefunction; more rapid variation means larger momentum and therefore larger kinetic energy.

p.src: Each value of $\ell$ defines a different radial operator because the centrifugal term changes with $\ell$. Thus $\ell=0,1,2,\ldots$ give separate radial towers. The positive centrifugal term shifts the levels upward as angular momentum is added. Every radial eigenvalue at fixed $\ell$ carries a magnetic multiplet of dimension $2\ell+1.$ The $\ell=0$ levels are singlets, the $\ell=1$ levels are triplets, and the $\ell=2$ levels are quintuplets. These are the degeneracies guaranteed by rotational symmetry; an additional symmetry may make states with different values of $\ell$ degenerate as well.

p.src: For atomic-type potentials satisfying $V(r)\to0$ at large $r$, the escape threshold is conventionally $E=0$. The negative-energy states form the discrete bound spectrum. At and above $E=0$, one encounters the scattering continuum. This statement depends on the large-$r$ behavior of the potential and does not apply to a confining central potential.

p.src: The exact nonrelativistic Coulomb potential has an additional alignment of levels. The lowest $\ell=1$ radial state has the same energy as the first excited $\ell=0$ state. The next $\ell=1$ state aligns with the second excited $\ell=0$ state, and the lowest $\ell=2$ state joins them. The pattern continues through the higher radial and angular-momentum towers.

en: The classical reduction placed a single orbit in a plane, but that step cannot be applied to a quantum wavefunction in the same way. A quantum orbital state fills three-dimensional space. The full angular operator is $L^2=L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2$, and its eigenvalue retains the three-dimensional result $\hbar^2\ell(\ell+1)$.

p.src: Small Oscillations and the Harmonic Oscillator

u.src: Small Oscillations and the Harmonic Oscillator
en: Small Oscillations and the Harmonic Oscillator

p.src: Near a stable equilibrium, a sufficiently small displacement often produces harmonic motion. The effective radial potential for nonzero angular momentum provides one example: radial motion close to the bottom of its well is approximately harmonic.

u.src: Near a stable equilibrium, a sufficiently small displacement often produces harmonic motion. The effective radial potential for nonzero angular momentum provides one example: radial motion close to the bottom of its well is approximately harmonic.
en: Near a stable equilibrium, a sufficiently small displacement often produces harmonic motion. The effective radial potential for nonzero angular momentum provides one example: radial motion close to the bottom of its well is approximately harmonic.

p.src:
Consider a one-dimensional oscillator with unit mass. Let $x$ be the displacement from equilibrium and write the spring constant as $k=\omega^2$. The classical Hamiltonian is $H=\frac{p^2}{2}+\frac{\omega^2x^2}{2}.$ Hamilton’s equations give $\dot{x}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p}=p,
\qquad
\dot{p}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}=-\omega^2x,$ and therefore $\ddot{x}=-\omega^2x.$ Thus $\omega$ is the classical oscillation frequency.

p.src: Factorization and the Zero-Point Energy

u.src: Factorization and the Zero-Point Energy
en: Factorization and the Zero-Point Energy

p.src:
Quantum mechanically, $=i\hbar.$ The Hamiltonian is a sum of squares, suggesting the factorization $\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2}(p+i\omega x)(p-i\omega x)
&=\frac{1}{2}\left(p^2+\omega^2x^2+i\omega[x,p]\right) \\
&=\frac{1}{2}\left(p^2+\omega^2x^2-\hbar\omega\right).\end{aligned}$ Hence $H=\frac{1}{2}(p+i\omega x)(p-i\omega x)
+\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega.$ The additive term $\hbar\omega/2$ is the zero-point energy.

p.src: Classically the lowest energy would occur at $x=p=0$. Quantum mechanically no state can have both position and momentum sharply fixed at zero. Moreover, the two terms $p^2/2$ and $\omega^2x^2/2$ are positive and cannot cancel. A nonzero ground-state energy is therefore unavoidable.

u.src: The Oscillator Ladder
en: The Oscillator Ladder

p.src: Define $N=A_+A_-.$ The Hamiltonian is then $H=\hbar\omega\left(N+\frac{1}{2}\right).$ Thus finding the energy spectrum reduces to finding the eigenvalues of $N$.

u.src: Define $N=A_+A_-.$ The Hamiltonian is then $H=\hbar\omega\left(N+\frac{1}{2}\right).$ Thus finding the energy spectrum reduces to finding the eigenvalues of $N$.
en: Define $N=A_+A_-.$ The Hamiltonian is then $H=\hbar\omega\left(N+\frac{1}{2}\right).$ Thus finding the energy spectrum reduces to finding the eigenvalues of $N$.

p.src:
Suppose $N|n\rangle=n|n\rangle.$ The commutators with $N$ are $\begin{aligned}
&=A_+[A_-,A_+]=A_+, \\
[N,A_-]
&=[A_+,A_-]A_-=-A_-.\end{aligned}$ It follows that $\begin{aligned}
N\bigl(A_+|n\rangle\bigr)
&=(n+1)A_+|n\rangle, \\
N\bigl(A_-|n\rangle\bigr)
&=(n-1)A_-|n\rangle.\end{aligned}$ Thus $A_+$ raises an eigenvalue of $N$ by one and $A_-$ lowers it by one whenever the resulting vector is nonzero.

p.src:
The operator $N$ is nonnegative: $\langle\psi|N|\psi\rangle
=\langle\psi|A_+A_-|\psi\rangle
=\|A_-|\psi\rangle\|^2
\geq0.$ The lowering process therefore cannot continue into negative eigenvalues. At a bottom state $|b\rangle$, it must terminate: $A_-|b\rangle=0.$

p.src:
For normalized eigenstates, the coefficients in the ladder are fixed by their norms: $\begin{aligned}
\|A_-|n\rangle\|^2
&=\langle n|A_+A_-|n\rangle=n, \\
\|A_+|n\rangle\|^2
&=\langle n|A_-A_+|n\rangle=n+1.\end{aligned}$ Phases may therefore be chosen so that $A_-|n\rangle=\sqrt{n}\,|n-1\rangle,
\qquad
A_+|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}\,|n+1\rangle.$

Starting from this lowest state and applying $A_+$ gives $n=0,1,2,\ldots.$ Restoring the additive zero-point term, the oscillator energies are $E_n=\hbar\omega\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right),
\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.$
